power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .054", "p = .836"), Sentence = c("One-sample t-tests confirmed that infants were able to discriminate both the frequent (m = 0.57, sd = 0.13, t(13) = 2.12, p = .054, d = 0.57) and the infrequent (m = 0.62, sd = 0.13, t(15) = 3.06, p = .003, d = 0.90) contrast (Figure 2).", "A one-sample t-test did not provide evidence for successful discrimination in this experiment (m = 0.49, sd = 0.15, t(25) = -0.21, p = .836, d = -0.041)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Many different models have been proposed to capture acoustic properties of speech -but which describes infant perception?
Discrimination scores were gathered from individual infants for two vowel contrasts.
These and other categories were subsequently elicited from each infant's primary caregiver.
Regression analyses were used to assess fit between individual variation in infant vowel discrimination, and auditory contrast estimates for the relevant and control contrasts in caregiver speech.
The latter were calculated using three models that have been proposed to capture speech: formants, RASTA-PLP and CASP.
None of these models were significantly related to infant discrimination scores, but a marginally significant negative correlation was observed for CASP.
As a follow-up, a second set of infant discrimination scores and caregiver productions was gathered, with the hope of evaluating CASP specifically.
However, due to a failure to replicate the previous discrimination results no further analyses were conducted.
A child growing up in an English-speaking household will come to have an English phonology, whereas a child growing up in a Dutch-speaking household will come to have a Dutch phonology.
This observation demonstrates that the input language a child receives plays a crucial role in the acquisition of speech categories.

Moreover, some research suggests that even fine-grained variation in the speech of individual caregivers is reflected in their infants' sound discrimination, such that infants' discrimination of sound contrasts is predicted from acoustical descriptions of their primary caregiver's speech [1, 2] .
text.formatted: Moreover, some research suggests that even fine-grained variation in the speech of individual caregivers is reflected in their infants' sound discrimination, such that infants' discrimination of sound contrasts is predicted from acoustical descriptions of their primary caregiver's speech <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">2]</ref> .

text.text: The present research sought to assess the potential psychological relevance of different acoustic models of speech by utilizing individual variation.
Individual variation is an increasingly common topic in infant research.

Most relevant to the current work are two recent behavioral studies documenting correlations between caregivers' speech and infant sound discrimination. [1] found that the infants of mothers with larger vowel spaces needed fewer trials to learn that a sound change from a background /Ci/ to an oddball /tCi/ predicted a reward in the conditioned headturn procedure.
text.formatted: Most relevant to the current work are two recent behavioral studies documenting correlations between caregivers' speech and infant sound discrimination. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[1]</ref> found that the infants of mothers with larger vowel spaces needed fewer trials to learn that a sound change from a background /Ci/ to an oddball /tCi/ predicted a reward in the conditioned headturn procedure.

text.text: While this correlational result remained open to a number of interpretations (e.g., the boost in performance follows from a more nourishing emotional environment which correlates with larger vowel spaces; see e.g., [3, 4]), subsequent work bolsters the hypothesis that individual variation in caregiver speech is reflected in infant perception.
text.formatted: While this correlational result remained open to a number of interpretations (e.g., the boost in performance follows from a more nourishing emotional environment which correlates with larger vowel spaces; see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">4]</ref>), subsequent work bolsters the hypothesis that individual variation in caregiver speech is reflected in infant perception.

text.text: For example, individual infants' ability to discriminate /s/ from /S/ was predicted by caregivers' clearer pronunciation of /s/, but not by higher pitched utterances, or slower speech rates [2].
text.formatted: For example, individual infants' ability to discriminate /s/ from /S/ was predicted by caregivers' clearer pronunciation of /s/, but not by higher pitched utterances, or slower speech rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[2]</ref>.

text.text: In order to truly understand the relationship between infants' categories and the input they experienced, it is necessary to describe that spoken input as it is perceived by the child.
This raises a key question: Which of the many acoustical and auditory models proposed to describe speech best predicts the association between input and representations?
In infant research, it is common to describe vowels in terms of their F1, F2, and duration, as [1] did.
text.formatted: In infant research, it is common to describe vowels in terms of their F1, F2, and duration, as <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[1]</ref> did.

text.text: Tools for automatic speech recognition (ASR) often rely on Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) or perceptual linear prediction (PLP) features.
These features represent more information from the signal than formants and so have been proposed to describe the statistical properties of infantdirected speech [5].
text.formatted: These features represent more information from the signal than formants and so have been proposed to describe the statistical properties of infantdirected speech <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Outside of direct applications to ASR, there exists a substantial literature on psychophysically accurate models of auditory perception, for instance models that simulate the anatomy of the human ear (cf. [6] for a recent overview).
text.formatted: Outside of direct applications to ASR, there exists a substantial literature on psychophysically accurate models of auditory perception, for instance models that simulate the anatomy of the human ear (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[6]</ref> for a recent overview).

text.text: Presumably, these models describe even more accurately the information extracted from the speech of infants' caregivers.

We sought an empirical answer to this key theoretical question here by using the association between individual variation in caregiver speech and infant perception as a test case to assess the descriptive value of a number of acoustic and auditory models.
The discrimination scores in a group of Dutch infants served as a proxy for their representation of a given vowel contrast.
Half of the infants was tested on the contrast between two highly frequent categories, /e/and /I/.
The other half responded to the contrast between the rather infrequent categories /ø/and /Y/.

The primary caregiver of each individual infant was subsequently recorded, using as elicitation stimuli common child-directed words that contained all of those 4 target vowels, in addition to a control contrast between /O/ and /o/.
We calculated divergence measures for each of these three contrasts using three models of speech audition.
Discrimination scores were then correlated to these production measures, which allowed us to assess the following predictions.
First, correlations were performed separately for the data of infants that had been exposed to the frequent contrast and infants that had been exposed to the infrequent contrast.

Thus, in the frequent correlations, vowel divergences were based on caregivers' productions of the frequent contrast, and in the infrequent model they were based on productions of the infrequent contrast.

We predicted that correlations should be overall less strong for the rare /ø/-/Y/vowels than for the frequent vowels, as infants have had less exposure to the former, and thus their discrimination should respond to a lesser extent to their caregivers' productions.

Second, to evaluate the effect of variables unrelated to the actual contrast, we also included correlations of the production data from the unrelated control contrast o-O, and the number of trials to habituation.
The control vowels provide a safety check in terms of caregivers' overall clarity of speech: There should be no difference in discriminability or predictive power based on the control /o-O/ contrast.
The number of trials to habituation are an indication of infants' attention to habituation stimuli (cf. [7]).
text.formatted: The number of trials to habituation are an indication of infants' attention to habituation stimuli (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[7]</ref>).

text.text: Third, we evaluated the main theoretical motivation of the present research: Which acoustic models best describe infants' input as they perceive it?
In order to do so, we included divergences of all three models in the correlations, in order to compare the degree to which they correlated with the discrimination data.

Indeed, it may be that e.g. proponents of CASP are entirely correct in that the best model of the input to the auditory cortex is well-described by their algorithm, in which case we expect the strongest correlation for the discrimination data and CASP.

However, it could also be the case that infants are sensitive to more than one representation, and when they hear their caregivers' speech they also perceive not only information captured by CASP but also, e.g., formants.

We predicted a positive relationship between divergences in maternal speech and discrimination, along the lines of previous work where mothers who produced more marked phonetic contrasts had infants who were better at discriminating those sounds.
>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: Forty-one infants were included in the final analysis.

Twenty-one of these infants were assigned to the frequent condition (8 females, age M = 6.10 months, range = 4.80 -6.80 months), and another twenty were assigned to the infrequent condition (11 females, age M = 6.57 months, range = 5.00 -7.66 months).

Eleven more infants did not contribute discrimination data due to fussiness (frequent: 5, infrequent: 2), failure to habituate (frequent: 2), experimenter error (infrequent: 1), dialectal language background (infrequent: 1).
We did not succeed in recording all caregivers of infants in the final sample.
For the dyads in the frequent group, 7 caregivers did not contribute recordings because of equipment error or data loss (6) or declining to record (1).
For the dyads in the infrequent group, 4 caregivers did not contribute recordings due to equipment error or data loss (2), infant fussiness during the recording session (1), or dialect (1).
All stimuli had been recorded in infant-directed speech by a female native Dutch talker, and its acoustic characteristics in F1-F2 space are portrayed in Figure 1.
text.formatted: All stimuli had been recorded in infant-directed speech by a female native Dutch talker, and its acoustic characteristics in F1-F2 space are portrayed in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: Both caregiver and experimenter, who coded infant looking online, were blinded to the auditory stimulation through loud music played over headphones.
Infants sat on their caregiver's lap in front of a large screen on which images were shown and from which sound was played.
Each trial began with a silent attention-getter (a video of a laughing baby).
When the infant fixated on the screen, a colorful bull's eye was displayed and the auditory stimulation began.
This stimulation continued until the end of the file was reached, or until the infant looked away for more than 2 consecutive seconds.
Time spent looking away was not counted in the overall tally.
There were two phases to this study.

During the habituation phase of the group exposed to the frequent contrast, which could last up to 24 trials, a single token of /hIt/ was repeated up to 17 times with 750 ms ISI, for a maximum trial duration of 20 seconds.
Habituation criterion was reached when the infant looking time averaged over Fig. 1.
text.formatted: Habituation criterion was reached when the infant looking time averaged over Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: Acoustic characteristics of the stimulus vowel contrasts in F1-F2 space the preceding 3 trials had fallen below 50% of the average of the 3 trials during which the child had looked the longest.
This event led to the onset of the test phase, which used the 'hybrid' paradigm because it has been found to capture individual variation in infant discrimination reliably [8].
text.formatted: This event led to the onset of the test phase, which used the 'hybrid' paradigm because it has been found to capture individual variation in infant discrimination reliably <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, there were 10 'same' trials, consisting of the habituated /hIt/ file, and 4 'alternating' trials, consisting of the alternation of the habituated /hIt/ token and a novel /het/ token.

The dependent measure entered in subsequent analyses was the looking ratio (average looking time during the first alternating trials divided by the sum of the average looking time during the first alternating and the first same trial), such that good discrimination should be reflected in values higher than .5.
The procedure was identical for the group exposed to the infrequent contrast, except that they were habituated to a single token of /hYt/, and subsequently tested on alternations of /hYt/ and /høt/.
Immediately after the discrimination study, the infant was turned slightly so that she could look both at the caregiver and at the screen.
The 'game' consisted of heralding a picture; thus, the caregiver read out loud a word written out on the screen, and immediately after this a picture corresponding to the word was shown.
The targets were chosen from high frequency words, with which most infants would be familiar and that caregivers would find natural to produce.
We elicited a total of 36 words, such that each of 6 target vowels was presented in 6 different lexical contexts.
The acoustical properties of the caregivers' speech is represented by three different feature representations.
The first representation, and arguably the one most common in infant perception research, is based on the formants of the vowels.
Formants F1 and F2 were automatically extracted from the caregivers' vowel productions using Praat [9].
text.formatted: Formants F1 and F2 were automatically extracted from the caregivers' vowel productions using Praat <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[9]</ref>.

text.text: The method proposed by [10] was used to determine suitable ceilings for stable formants per speaker and per vowel.
text.formatted: The method proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[10]</ref> was used to determine suitable ceilings for stable formants per speaker and per vowel.

text.text: Formants were converted to a Bark scale to reflect the logarithmic nature of auditory perception.
Vowels were represented as the average of the F1 and F2 over the middle third of the signal.

The acoustic divergence between two clusters of vowel productions was taken to be the Euclidean distance between the means of the formants for each vowel cluster, similar to what is commonly done in infant perception research (cf. [11]).
text.formatted: The acoustic divergence between two clusters of vowel productions was taken to be the Euclidean distance between the means of the formants for each vowel cluster, similar to what is commonly done in infant perception research (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[11]</ref>).

text.text: The second feature representation that was used is perceptual linear prediction (PLP) [12] with relative spectra (RASTA) filtering [13].
text.formatted: The second feature representation that was used is perceptual linear prediction (PLP) <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[12]</ref> with relative spectra (RASTA) filtering <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[13]</ref>.

text.text: This is a common repre-sentation of acoustic features in automatic speech recognition (ASR).
Linear predictive analysis models the vocal tract using all pole transfer functions.
It models closely the high-energy spectral areas of the signal and smooths out the harmonic structure and noisy details.
PLP combines this approach with spectral warping techniques to model the non-linear frequency sensitivity of human hearing.
The RASTA filtering technique filters in the log domain of the power spectrum to compensates for channel effects.
In our implementation, a 12th order PLP model with a 25ms window with a 10ms shift was extracted from the speech signal.
The resultant feature frames had 27 elements.
The divergence measure between vowel clusters is described below.
The last model used was based on the Computational Auditory Signal Processing and Perception (CASP) model proposed in [6].
text.formatted: The last model used was based on the Computational Auditory Signal Processing and Perception (CASP) model proposed in <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[6]</ref>.

text.text: This model consists of several stages.

The first are the outer and middle ear transformations, implemented by two finite impulse response (FIR) filters, modeling the transfer function from the outer ear to the eardrum and the mechanical impedance change from outer ear to middle ear, respectively.
The second stage is a dual resonance non-linear filter bank, designed to mimic the basilar membrane response behavior, based on animal observations.
The third stage simulates hair-cell transduction stage of the transfer of basilar membrane oscillations into neural receptor potentials.
Lastly, these potentials are combined with noise into a modulation processing stage simulating the results from physiological recordings (for full details of the model see [6]).
text.formatted: Lastly, these potentials are combined with noise into a modulation processing stage simulating the results from physiological recordings (for full details of the model see <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[6]</ref>).

text.text: In our implementation, the output from the last modulation filter bank was de-correlated using a discrete cosine transform (DCT) with 13 components.
The last model is arguably the most complex.
Its processing paths are based on detailed observations about the processes underlying human hearing up to the neuronal level.
The model is further validated with tone detection and discrimination experiments [14].
text.formatted: The model is further validated with tone detection and discrimination experiments <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[14]</ref>.

text.text: While this is not a model tuned for speech processing, it is interesting to see how it measures up against the above models that have been explicitly tuned for speech.
In our use of the RASTA-PLP and CASP models, no averaging over frames took place and the entire temporal range of the signal was preserved (unlike in the formants model).

Although the vowels used in this paper are not known for changing rapidly over time like diphthongs, we chose to preserve the full temporal dynamics of the signal and made no assumptions on the extraction of static parts by the infant, as in commonly done in ASR, where multiple states are used to represent the temporal dynamics of phonemes.
The divergence measure used here reflects this choice.

In the infant language acquisition literature, various measures for the distances between vowel clusters have been proposed, ranging from the simple, e.g. the difference between cluster means proposed by [11], to the more complex, e.g. taking into account the possible heteroscedasticity of the data [2].
text.formatted: In the infant language acquisition literature, various measures for the distances between vowel clusters have been proposed, ranging from the simple, e.g. the difference between cluster means proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[11]</ref>, to the more complex, e.g. taking into account the possible heteroscedasticity of the data <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[2]</ref>.

text.text: In all these proposals, vowel tokens are summarized by the static middle of the tokens.
Duration, if it is considered, is brought into the model as an additional feature.
For the RASTA-PLP and CASP models, we took a different approach.
Durational differences between vowel tokens were modeled implicitly by using dynamic time warping (DTW) as the token-to-token divergence measure.
Unnormalized DTW without path constraints takes into account a nonlinear measure of differences in duration, expressed as the incremental summation over frame distances.
This approach implies that the weight of the latent duration feature is determined on a per-token-pair basis, being integrated in the divergence measure.
For the divergence measure between vowel clusters, average linkage was used, i.e. the mean of the pairwise token-to-token divergences between the clusters.

One-sample t-tests confirmed that infants were able to discriminate both the frequent (m = 0.57, sd = 0.13, t(13) = 2.12, p = .054, d = 0.57) and the infrequent (m = 0.62, sd = 0.13, t(15) = 3.06, p = .003, d = 0.90) contrast (Figure 2).
text.formatted: One-sample t-tests confirmed that infants were able to discriminate both the frequent (m = 0.57, sd = 0.13, t(13) = 2.12, p = .054, d = 0.57) and the infrequent (m = 0.62, sd = 0.13, t(15) = 3.06, p = .003, d = 0.90) contrast (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>).

text.text: The discrimination results of the full sample are reported elsewhere [15].
text.formatted: The discrimination results of the full sample are reported elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[15]</ref>.

text.text: In order to evaluate the relationship between the three models of audition described above and the discrimination results, we performed Pearson's correlations separately for (1) the data of infants that had been exposed to the frequent contrast and (2) infants that had been exposed to the infrequent contrast.
We included the discrimination data of infants exposed to the frequent contrast in the frequent correlations.
These data were correlated to vowel divergences based on their caregivers' productions of the frequent contrast.
For the infrequent correlations, the discrimination data of infants exposed to the infrequent contrast were correlated to distances based on their caregivers' productions of the infrequent contrast.
In addition, in order to account for the influence of individual caregivers' speech clarity, distances based on the control contrasts were added to both correlations.
Individual differences in infants' attention to the stimuli (cf. [7]) were accounted for by additionally correlating the distance measures to length of habituation.
text.formatted: Individual differences in infants' attention to the stimuli (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[7]</ref>) were accounted for by additionally correlating the distance measures to length of habituation.

text.text: Thus, individual infants' discrimination scores and habituation lengths were correlated to the three types of distance measures for the frequent or infrequent contrast and the control contrast, resulting in a 2*6 correlation matrix for both the frequent and the infrequent correlations.
Multiple comparisons were Holm-adjusted.
As can be seen in Table 1, there were no significant correlation effects.
text.formatted: As can be seen in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, there were no significant correlation effects.

text.text: As for our main theoretical question, we found that no model was significantly related to infant discrimination scores.

Despite this negative result (which could be due to the small sample size, see Conclusion section), one curious outcome was that descriptively, the strongest effect we found was a negative relation between distances based on CASP and infant discrimination scores (which would have been significant if we had not corrected for multiple comparisons).

Since the direction of this result contradicted previous findings, and to allow a targeted evaluation of CASP measures only (thus avoiding the need for multiple comparison correction), we decided to replicate the experiment with the frequent vowel contrast.
Twenty-six infants were included in the final analysis ( nation data due to fussiness.
text.formatted: Twenty-six infants were included in the final analysis <ref type="bibr">(</ref> nation data due to fussiness.

text.text: Stimuli and procedure for both the discrimination experiment and recording session were identical to those of the group of infants previously tested on the frequent contrast, and the experiment was conducted with exactly the same equipment in the same laboratory.
The only difference was the experimenter, who changed from a well-trained experimenter in the previous experiments to a newly trained one in the replication experiment.
A one-sample t-test did not provide evidence for successful discrimination in this experiment (m = 0.49, sd = 0.15, t(25) = -0.21, p = .836, d = -0.041).
Since we failed to replicate the overall discrimination result, we did not code nor analyze the parental speech as it was unclear that the infant discrimination data was reliable.

In the current study, we tested the main predictions (1) that the relationship between caregiver productions and infant discrimination performance should be more evident in a frequently than an infrequently heard contrast and (2) that some auditory models would be better fit to describe infants' input as they perceive it.
We did not find evidence for either prediction, and if anything, we found descriptive evidence in the opposite direction, with distances being negatively correlated with discrimination.
The null result itself could be due to several reasons.
First, it is possible that there is no relationship between caregiver productions and infant perception abilities.
That is, however, unlikely given that previous research shows such an association both for vowels and consonants [1, 2].
text.formatted: That is, however, unlikely given that previous research shows such an association both for vowels and consonants <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">2]</ref>.

text.text: Second, since we based one of our models on a measure similar to that used in a previous study, it is also unlikely that our choice of distance measures caused our results.
A third possible reason is that our choice of vowel contrast was not suited to capture individual variation, even more so since we failed to replicate the discrimination results themselves.
The failure to replicate the results with a slightly larger sample could indicate that our first result was a false positive.
It is also possible that the newly trained experimenter performed poorly in the online coding task.
Finally, a fourth possibility is that our small sample had too little power to elicit significant results, especially given the relative large number of multiple comparisons we performed.
Without further experiments it will not be possible to tease apart these possibilities.
